# Introduction to RPA and Microsoft Power Automate

## Overview
RPA (Robotic Process Automation) is a major branch of the automation world that you must understand, because many enterprises rely on it and it is a common job requirement. RPA tools - the big names are UiPath, Automation Anywhere, and Microsoft Power Automate - create software 'robots' that mimic a human interacting with applications: clicking, typing, copying between screens, and reading data from interfaces. This is essential in large organizations full of legacy or desktop software that has no API, where the only way to automate is to drive the user interface, much like the browser automation you learned but extended to desktop apps and structured with enterprise features. A key distinction is attended vs unattended automation: attended bots run alongside a human, triggered on demand to assist with a task, while unattended bots run entirely on their own on a server, often on a schedule, doing high-volume back-office work. Microsoft Power Automate is the most accessible RPA-adjacent tool for beginners because it has a generous free tier, integrates deeply with Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Excel, Teams, SharePoint), and offers both cloud flows (like Zapier/Make for connecting online services) and desktop flows (true RPA that controls your Windows applications). The professional judgment to develop is when RPA is the right choice: if a clean API exists, API-based automation (Zapier/Make/n8n/scripts) is faster, cheaper, and more reliable, so RPA should be reserved for systems where UI interaction is the only option. Understanding RPA rounds out your toolkit and lets you speak the language of enterprise automation teams.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: What RPA is (UiPath, Automation Anywhere, Power Automate); Attended vs unattended automation; Power Automate cloud flows; Desktop automation and UI interaction; When RPA beats API-based automation. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Create a free Microsoft account and build a Power Automate cloud flow (e.g., when an email with an attachment arrives, save it to OneDrive and post a Teams message), then run and test it.
Mini Project: Build a small Power Automate solution combining a cloud flow and, if possible, a desktop flow: for example, on a schedule, read rows from an Excel file, process them, and record results back - or trigger a desktop task that a UI-only app requires.
Assignment: Explain the difference between attended and unattended RPA and write a decision note on when you would choose RPA over an API-based tool, with two concrete examples.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
